utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The affirmation you made at the beginning of your evidence to tell the truth still applies, Mr. Peraj. Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Peraj. I will not be taking too much of your time. I told you my next topic is Mr. Seregj Perovic. This is the man, you say you mentioned him for the first time in the Milutinovic case, and after that this person appears in your statement after the amendments that you wanted to do. You wanted to amend Major Zivkovic, the name that was there, and you wanted it replaced with Seregj Perovic. You explained to us who he was, and you explained to us why you didn't do that before, and why, in fact, the first time that you did it was in the Milutinovic case. And you say the first reason was of a humanitarian nature. That person assisted, helped 100 people survive. You said that there were more than 100 people who saw you with him and that people to this day asked you to say thank you to Seregj Perovic for what he did. You said that the second reason why you never mentioned his name was the fact that he had called you on the phone and asked you to forget about his name, to cut a long story short. Now, my short question is regarding Sergegj Perovic is this: Why did you do that in the Milutinovic case if you were so certain that this man assisted your compatriots and if you new that this man risked his life. You described this man as a humane person, and he had asked you to -- not to reveal his name, yet you betrayed him in a way. So what was the motive for that? Could you please tell us.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: First, I've not betrayed anyone. I mentioned his name because, in my opinion, the circumstances, the political circumstances have changed, so I thought that his life was no longer at risk. This is the reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Is it something that you thought, or did you talk to him and did he tell you that?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he did not say that to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I will have no other questions regarding Seregj Perovic. Now could you please look at paragraph 70 of your statement of the 8th and 9th of August. It's already been admitted into evidence. It says --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the counsel please slow down when reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 70, you can see this paragraph. You say: "I was on the KLA list for liquidation and the MUP obtained it in the course of a search in Dobos. I was shown this list by Captain Perovic." Could you please tell me, have you ever learned why you were on that list, what was the reason? And is it, indeed, true that you were on this list?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This I learned from Seregj Perovic. I have not seen the list myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I am not able to find the paragraph, Mr. Djordjevic. Paragraph 70?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nor can I.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, Your Honour. Just a moment. Well, I obviously provided you with the wrong reference, but to speed things up, I will give you the reference later, and the witness has already told us that Perovic had told him that. I will look for the exact reference and provide it at a later stage, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Let me now move on to the part of your statement when you talk about your amended statement that you gave on the 17th of February, 2009. It's an overview of additional information. And let me draw your attention to paragraph 8 in the additional information where you talk about the jerry-cans or canisters. And you say in the third and the sixth sentence in the statement that I already quoted, it says: "Major Zivkovic should be replaced by Captain First Class Seregj Perovic." That's between the seventh and eighth sentence. The additional sentence should be added: "About 2 or 3 metres away from the bodies I saw two jerry-cans with fuel and a heap torn documents, ID cards and passports." That's paragraph 73 of the statement that you gave previously and that you then amended. Now I'm going to ask you to answer this: Why is it that you do that for the first time today, that you mention that you saw those jerry-cans there; and secondly, the ID cards? Since this is a very important piece of information when we're talking about the allegations in the indictment, you've never mentioned that before.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I respond?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have mentioned it already earlier. I don't know exactly in which statement, because I have given several statements to the Tribunal investigators, so I don't remember to whom. But what I know is that I've already mentioned it earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Secondly, let us move on to paragraph 85 of the same statement and the supplement, the additional information, that you provided on the 17th of February, 2009, to the Court. You say in paragraph 85: "Some of the witnesses mentioned in Meje, before executing people, the Serbs would spray a gas to incapacitate the victims before execution. I did see one of the paramilitary soldiers carrying a gas mask near the execution site." And then you go on to say: "I never saw any gas canisters in Meje to confirm this allegation, but I'm convinced that the Serbs used them ..." and so on. In the supplement, paragraph 6, third sentence, you say: "The third sentence in paragraph 85 should read: 'I never saw any jerry-cans with fuel in Meje to confirm this, but I'm sure that the Serbs used them.'" And you say that this sentence should read as follows: "Three jerry-cans with fuel that I saw in Meje ..."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please repeat the last part of his sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: So your evidence here is not consistent, so could you please tell us what is it all about? You talk about fuel canisters or jerry-cans in the supplement paragraph 8, and then you say in paragraph 85 of your statement of the 8th and 9th of August that you heard that those were gas canisters. And then again in supplement, in paragraph 16, although you see in paragraph 85 that you never saw those canisters, now you say that you did see them. And then I'm asking you to explain --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We've had at least six questions now. You're going on and on with questions. And I would also point out that on Friday you asked for five extra minutes, we said you could have ten. You have now have 15. So clarify your canisters, and that will be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is my last question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: This is my last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So now I would like you to explain those illogicalities in your statements, the discrepancies between your initial statement and the additional statements. So are we talking about jerry-cans or canisters with fuel or gas canisters? What is it that you actually saw? Could you please tell us that.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: They're canisters with fuel or benzene, but I'm not talking about them. I'm talking about canisters with toxic gas, chemical gas, to poison people. This is a very small canister. They wanted to spray the son of my brother. This is what I wanted to explain to you. If you can allow me to continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I could tell you that the coffins of the people who were -- that the bodies of the people who were executed, the bodies which were lying near the cemetery, I did not see the bodies, but I saw the blood spots and the blood streams. They seemed to be like the stains made by a football ball. They were big stains of blood, the size of a football ball. So I assumed that if they did not use such a gas, then during the execution, the people would have fallen on the left or on the right. But actually, they were all lined up. Also, the blood spots would not have been lined in three lines. They were symmetrical, just -- they had the same size. The blood on the grass of the meadow was dry, and in that place there was no grass for two years. I was personally told by Major Zivkovic that the gas was used. He was in Meje on that day, but he was not with me. He was with another team. So he confirmed this to me. Also, the son of my brother talked to me about this. In my declaration I have said that I've not seen people using it. I've not seen people holding such cans. As far as the gas masks are concerned, then I could tell you that I've seen the soldier, a paramilitary, with a gas mask. I have also seen other people with gas masks which they had tied to their right foot, the gas masks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Djordjevic, there was quite a bit given there that didn't directly flow from your question. If you want to ask some further question from that answer, you may before you need to sit down.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. My question will be this: Why has the witness never mentioned that at all, the ID cards? And he was quite specific about not having seen the canisters. Why does he now change his evidence and say that he did see them? Because he's never said that before, yet he signed the statement. And it is quite clearly stated there that he had never seen them, and yet in the supplement he changes everything, and why does he again say the same thing today in court?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can you assist us there, please, Mr. Peraj?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I did mention this before in my statement. I'm more than sure I did. I am saying this.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I have to interrupt you. Please look at paragraph --

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Honourable Judge can maybe interrupt my --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Peraj, can you please look at paragraph 85.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judges, I don't want to get answers to questions that I never asked. That is why I would like the witness to look at paragraph 85 of the statement that he gave and that he signed, and to tell me why is it that he said this at that time and then changed his statement in the supplement and now. This is my last question, if the witness wants to give me an answer. Could he please look at the statement and then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, I will put the question. In paragraph 85, Mr. Peraj, you said: "I never saw gas canisters in Meje to confirm this, but I am convinced that the Serbs used them." Did you see gas canisters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, yes, I did see them with my own eyes, and you can hold me morally, legally, responsible for my claim.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Where were you when you saw them, the gas canisters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was in Meje. Just close to the bodies was a pile of documents that had been burnt down, and there was one small canister near the pile of documents and two other gas canisters a little bit further away, thrown on the grass.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can you then tell us how you came to say in this statement in paragraph 85 that "I never saw gas canisters in Meje"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I honestly don't know. I did mention that before. When all my statements were summarised into one, maybe there was a change, not a deliberate change. But believe me, what I'm telling you here now is true, and you can hold me responsible for that. I'm 100 percent sure that that was the case. I saw them myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And it is also your belief that you had said this in earlier statements, is that correct, that you had seen the canisters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did mention it in my earlier statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And you don't know how this change occurred in paragraph 85 for you to say "I never saw gas canisters in Meje"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I said, I was a little bit confused with the interpretation - gas canisters, fuel canisters. It is true that you can carry fuel and petrol in canisters. There are -- there is also gas used to burn bodies, and I did mention that I did not see such type of gas. This canister can hold 10, 20 litres in it, and I did not see that type of canister.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Did you see fuel canisters, fuel cans, in Meja, holding benzene, petrol?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's why the word "canister" is a little bit confusing. I did not see fuel cans or petrol cans in Meje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Djordjevic, I think we have reached the end, well and truly the end of the time that you should spend in the cross-examination, so thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I just wanted to note that in the supplement the witness again spoke about fuel cans, not about gas canisters, in paragraph 8 and further on in the supplement. That's all. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That's a matter we can look at in due course. Do we have an exhibit number for the statement of the 17th of February, 2009, the supplement or the amendment of the earlier statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. That was just a supplementary information sheet containing what the witness said in proofing which we gave to the Defence, so we alerted him in chief to the change that he wanted to make to the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: As it has been the subject of the continuing questioning, Mr. Stamp, you might, in the course of your re-examination, think to tender that so we can understand better what was being put to the witness, because we have not seen it so far.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that this is not usual practice for the supplementary statements given by the witnesses to be tendered into evidence. That is why we did not put it on our list of documents to be tendered and it's not in e-court. But in order for the Trial Chamber to get a full picture of this cross-examination, we will seek to tender this into evidence, and we will upload it into e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Djordjevic. I was hoping that Mr. Stamp had it already in his e-court list. Not so?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, then, we'll very much accept Mr. Djordjevic's offer. Thank you. And it will be received, and it will receive an exhibit number when you're able to tender it, and the Court Officer might now indicate the number it will receive.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be D00034, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Peraj.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When you were speaking of canisters that you saw, or a canister that you saw, what type of canister are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: These canister were of a size usually used in medicine for those who have problems with breathing. They were very small. In my opinion, they obtained toxic gas with a short-term use of effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And this is precisely what you told us in your statement.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what I said. JUDE PARKER: What statement was that --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That was the statement of the 8th and 9th of August, 2006, which is Exhibit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And where is the reference?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Paragraph 85, in the last sentence he said his nephew --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can I point out that the earlier reference in paragraph 85 which has been the subject of questioning, Mr. Stamp --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- was in the physical context of the execution site, and then what you are now referring to is a check-point at another place and another time that day where a policeman, or someone, was seen with a canister and about to administer the incapacitating agent.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I just wanted for the moment for that question. Thank you very much, Your Honour, to establish that he was referring to, I think, to an incapacitating agent. I'll get to the place presently.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It was put to you today that you had never spoken about seeing any gas canister at Meja before you made the change on the 17th of February when you spoke with attorneys from the OTP. I'd like to read to you part of a transcript of your testimony on the 15th of August, 2006. You were asked: "Do you still claim that gas was used in Meje?"

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And may I just give the reference, I don't think we should put the hundreds of pages of transcripts into testimony. I would just like to give the reference. This is page 1713 of the transcript in the Milutinovic et al case, and I'm quoting from paragraphs 10 to 18. And this is just to rebut the allegation that he recently, very recently, 17th of February this year, said that he saw a canister.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The question put to you was: "Do you still claim that gas was used in Meje?" And the answer: "Yes, I still abide by my claim for these reasons. Number 1, the person, I mentioned I changed the name, and I explained the reasons that I changed the name. He said he could smell an unusual smell, which is a chemical smell." The second reason -- I'm sorry. "He said he could smell an unusual smell, which was a chemical smell." "The second reason is that I saw with my own eyes a small canister. It was just like the one that people, people who suffer from asthma use. It was that size." Do you recall saying that three years ago almost?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could move on to something else quickly. You said, in answer to a question that my friend asked, that you did not report to Major Djosan the crimes that you witnessed on the 27th and the 28th because the person you were with and others must have reported them to him. Why do you say in the context of what was happening that they must have reported to him what was happening?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because a commander has his own assistant for morale and political issues, for security issues, assistant for information, assistant for personnel, so these were structures within the army that are duty-bound to report. And that's why I am more than sure that they must have informed him. If I, as an Albanian, informed him for Albanian victims, I don't think that -- I don't think that that would have gone on well. But, as I said, in a conversation with him -- a conversation with him, he did express his concerns about what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said that over the period of time you were in Djakovica, Major Djosan initiated proceedings against various persons.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Colonel, colonel, colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Excuse me, Colonel Djosan initiated proceedings against some VJ members of crimes, i.e., looting and theft, et cetera. What happened to these cases that Colonel Djosan brought against these people?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know, five persons were convicted. I don't know about others being convicted, though. However, those who were convicted were released after a short time, and this was upon somebody's orders. This would be my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we could move on to the paramilitaries. You said that Arkan's men, or the members of the Arkan unit, were always in the company of the police. Is this something that you observed yourself, or were you told about it?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is something I observed myself, especially in Meje, and at every check-point. There was a check-point at Brekoc, and whenever I would pass by, I would see such persons there. But in Meje I saw them with my own eyes. I will mention one thing to you. I did not see paramilitaries at the command post in Duzhnje, not even near the command itself. But in Meje, in Orize, yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said that Seselj's units were also involved in Meja and in Korenica, and you went on to say that they were also in the town of Djakovica itself, looting houses and setting them alight. Can you just elaborate further on what was happening in Djakovica with Seselj's unit? When, that is approximately when, and what did they do?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: They lived and were stationed in the town itself, near the location where we were as an army. I could see them in a cafe just close to the army centre. They were in action, so to say, the whole night. Every night they will loot, and then in the morning they would sleep late, until 2.00, 3.00 p.m. You could not see them in the morning. Afterwards they would gather again in this cafe. They would sing nationalist songs, and then they would go out for action again. I saw with my own eyes the houses that were burnt near the bus station. In the morning -- in the evening, correction, police or people dressed in police uniforms were standing by the asphalt road, while these men were involved in burning the houses down. I requested from Colonel Milos Djosan that something be undertaken against this, because this location was very close to the army location. But he said to me, This is not your business and not our business at all; this is somebody else's business. As you can see, I didn't provide so many details in the past because I wasn't asked about the details. That's why I'm telling you that I know what I'm saying, and you can hold me responsible morally and legally for my claims here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know of the police in Djakovica doing anything to restrain the paramilitaries in these activities that they were conducting - I think you called them actions - in these actions that they were conducting?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my knowledge, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In respect to the Frenkis, you said that they had a special -- or Frenki was a commander for special unit, a special anti-terrorist unit. Was his unit affiliated to any official organisation, as far as you know, that is, Frenki's unit?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had heard even before that this unit joined these operations based on an agreement between the Ministry of Defence and the Ministry of the Interior. There was an agreement, just like in Bosnia and Croatia. There was a previous agreement. However, later on, as far as I know, these agreements were not abided by properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Let's turn and focus on Colonel Kovacevic, who you said became the chief of the SUP, that is, the secretariat of the interior for Djakovica municipality and the neighbouring municipalities. You said that he was assigned to coordinate the actions of the MUP with the paramilitaries, and you also said that the MUP supported and coordinated their actions, or supported and coordinated the actions of the paramilitaries, and you saw this especially in Meja and in the town of Djakovica. Could you elaborate a little bit further. What, to your understanding, was Colonel Kovacevic's role in coordinating the paramilitaries and the MUP?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: If there was no cooperation, no agreement, the MUP would then prevent the actions undertaken by these forces. This is the proof. The MUP would prevent their actions and their crimes. Same can be said for the army. They would prevent the actions. Why, then, they did not prevent these structures from undertaking such inhumane actions, criminal actions? There were sufficient military and police forces to prevent their activities, the activities of these groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. You did tell us that police were present at the bus station while Seselj's Eagles were setting people's houses alight. You also said yesterday, and I think I should just read this question: "Do you have any knowledge of Frenki's men participating in any actions?" And your answer was: "I did not hear an operation in which the parties participated on their own." When they participated in actions, with whom would they normally act? You said he did not participate on their own, so I assume you mean this acted in coordination with another organisation. What are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my knowledge, they did not operate on their own. They were in coordination mainly with the police but with the army as well, especially with the intelligence and secret service structures of these two organisations. This is what I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, as a result of the -- or in light of what you described was happening in Djakovica, and that is the actions of the various paramilitaries, sometimes in the presence of the police, did the civilian Albanian population of Djakovica remain in the town after the 25th of March, 1999? Or during the NATO intervention, did the civilian Albanian population of Djakovica town remain there?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The majority of the population as a whole, Albanian and other ethnicities, was in Gjakove and the surrounding villages. There were also groups of civilians who left during this period of time. However, the greatest exodus was in April 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, with your leave, I'd like to show to the witness a photograph of a person and ask him if he recognises that person or if that person is related to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I take it this arises out of cross-examination, Mr. Stamp?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: He was asked to describe, and if I tell you where it arises, I'll be hinting to the witness where --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you show it to the Defence counsel before you ...

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wonder why this document has not been tendered earlier and it's only being done today, so that is the basis for our objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stamp has indicated already that he's doing it because of specific questions put by you, so we should allow him to continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Peraj, could you have a look at that photograph and tell me if the person depicted in it is familiar to you.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It seems to me that I must have seen this person, but I do not recall who he is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You were asked to describe the general that you saw at the MUP field headquarters, the general in charge of the special forces --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness has said -- the witness said that he couldn't recognise the person in the photograph, and now the Prosecutor is leading him by these words that he's just said to describe or to actually name the person, and that is the basis for our objection. The witness clearly said that he couldn't recognise the person, he couldn't remember who it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I was waiting a moment longer, Mr. Stamp, because it was not altogether clear what your line of questioning now is, but it certainly bears the interpretation suggested by Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is that what you're about, still pursuing the identity of the person in the photograph?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, you've had the witness's answer, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, he says it looks like someone he knows, but he cannot --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: No, he said: "I must have seen this fellow, but I don't know --"

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: "... but I don't recall who he is."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm trying to refresh his memory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, I think you'll have to leave that alone, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is that the end of your re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That was my last question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Peraj, you'll be pleased to know that that concludes the questions for you. The Chamber would thank you for your attendance here and the assistance you've given. In particular, we regret that it was necessary for you to stay over the weekend, but the additional evidence you've been able to give this morning will be of assistance to us. So you are now free to return to your wife and your ordinary activities, and we thank you for your assistance. And the Court Officer will show you out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I wish you good work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The next witness, if I understand correctly, Mr. Stamp or Mr. Neuner -- Mr. Neuner.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Neuner will be leading the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Is one that has protective measures; is that correct? Because of that, it will be necessary for us to adjourn to enable those to be put in place. Before we do, we would point out that the time anticipated in the Prosecution list for this witness was one hour. I mention that because, for all witnesses to date, the Prosecution has spent one and a half to two times longer than anticipated with the witness, and it will be necessary for us to give closer attention to timing. So, Mr. Neuner, we've put you on notice. And of course we will be conscious of the time spent in cross-examination as well because to date we have completed 11 witnesses in just over four weeks. At that rate of progress, this will be a very, very long trial, and we need now to, as things are getting more organised and everybody is becoming more familiar with the case and the issues that may be important, we will expect counsel to be able to focus more positively and concisely on the issues that really do matter in the case, and so we anticipate that the rate of progress will now become much quicker. And we encourage counsel to that end, and we will be monitoring progress from now on much more closely. And if we detect that time is being spent on matters that seem to be of little or no real importance in the case, we will be intervening to urge counsel to get on to matters that do matter. Now, having said that, looking at the time, I think the practical course for us would be to have the half-hour break now rather than the 20 minutes that would be necessary to put the security measures in place. And if we have a half-hour break now, we should be able to have two clear sessions of about an hour and a quarter for the rest of the sitting. Very well. We'll adjourn now, resuming at 10.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Neuner.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Good morning. The next witness is K90. He is a protected witness, and has next to the pseudonym image and voice distortion, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The witness is about to come in, so we'll move into closed session to enable that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: With the assistance of the usher, could I have the pseudonym sheet distributed first to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And, Witness, just read it and -- read it silently. Don't read it out aloud, please, and tell us whether you agree with it.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Could you please show it to the Defence as well. I would ask that this be tendered. The 65 ter number is 2631. And I would ask that it be tendered under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P00319, under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Could we now please have 65 ter 2646 being displayed to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Witness, it is correct you gave initially a statement in December 2002, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember the month, but that may be the case, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And when you came ...

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Maybe it is advisable to move into closed session because the first page of this statement which is being displayed may reveal the witness's name, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We have just arranged not to display the statement beyond this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: When you gave this statement, Witness -- if you have a look at it, it is displayed in front of you on the screen. We see the date is 31st of January, 2007. This is the last day of your testimony in the Milutinovic case. Is it correct that you made some changes already during the Milutinovic case to your statement?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And when you came a few days ago, you had some additional changes; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I want to walk you briefly through these changes, which we are doing here just on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Could we go in English and B/C/S to page 6, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And I'm referring you to paragraph 29. You told us in the second sentence that you wanted to have the word "Brigade" changed to "within my battalion." Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: If we could go in English to page 7 and B/C/S to page 8, please, and I'm referring now, if it comes, to paragraph 42, the fifth sentence. Actually, in English we need --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: One moment. In English we need to go to the next page, please. It's page 8, then. Yes. If we could maybe focus here in English on paragraphs 42 to 43, if I could impose my goodwill on the usher. I think that's enough. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I'm referring to the fifth sentence here. The word which is used there is "expel" and is it correct that you told us that you wanted to have the word "expel" changed to "relocate" in the fifth sentence?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And I'm now moving on to paragraph 43, the first and the third sentence, and I'm more or less referring here only to the B/C/S version because the English appear to be correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: You told us that you wanted to have the verb "proterivanje," which means expel in English, be replaced with the word "premestiti" which means relocate; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And this would -- if we could swap in B/C/S to the next page, please, paragraph 44.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: This same change you told us would also apply to the first sentence in paragraph 44.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Sorry, we have only English versions now. We would need the B/C/S version here, yeah. Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I'm following the changes that are being made now, in accordance with the supplementary information that I received. Under Roman numeral I, the last paragraph is 43. Mr. Neuner now moved on to 44. That's why I rose to ask what was this all about. I simply don't know. There is no such paragraph under Roman numeral I in this information. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I can clarify this very briefly. If you look, my learned colleague, if you look at the fourth hyphen, it starts with paragraph 43, the first and third sentences which I have just corrected, and paragraph 44, first sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise, but in the translation provided to me by the OTP - I don't know about the English version; I'll have a look now - I do not have a paragraph 44, just paragraph 43. I do apologise. Could I please just have a look. I've found the English version, too, Your Honour. Roman numeral I, you don't have paragraph 44 either. Well, let's see what the witness is going to change and then -- well, let's see, rather, what he's going to state, and then we'll proceed, will we? What do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The Chamber doesn't have these corrections at all, but what Mr. Neuner had indicated is that the same change would be made in paragraph 44 which had been made in paragraph 43, so it's the same change repeated.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Yeah. We have ERNed our supplementary information sheet, and I believe the ERN version has been communicated to you. I have the English version in front of me, which, in the fourth hyphen, contains these references to paragraph 43, first and third sentence; and paragraph 44, first sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Would you move on to deal with 44, then, and we'll see if there's still a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Yeah. It is, as Your Honour has pointed out, indeed the same change.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: If you look at paragraph 44, the first sentence, in B/C/S you wanted to have changed the word "proterivanje" to "promestiti."

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Yeah. In English it means basically from -- we change from "expel" to "relocate." And if we could go back to your last change, which is paragraph 43, the third sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: In the B/C/S version we'd need to go back now, please, one page. If you could highlight this, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: The third sentence, you wanted to have the phrase "sve primoramo" replaced by "im naredimo."

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: With these changes being undertaken, can I take that the statement now adequately reflects what you have stated and observed in 1999, in April?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Could I ask, Your Honours, with this explanation given, that 02646, the statement of the witness, could be tendered under seal, and we have also prepared for public version 02652, which contains some redactions, Your Honours. Could I ask that both statements be tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The statements will be received with the redactions in one version, and the unredacted version, under seal, for the other.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The under-seal version, Your Honours, will be assigned P00320, under seal. And the redacted version will be under P00321, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I now would like to move on to your testimony, which has the 65 ter number 5118. As I mentioned earlier, it was given on three days from the 29th to the 31st of January, 2007, in the Milutinovic case. Would you agree that the statements we just tendered, together with this testimony, accurately reflect what you would have -- what you would say if you give your testimony orally before this Court today?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: The testimony is the protocol, verbatim protocol. That's why I believe it's exactly what you have said. So I hope you agree that it doesn't only reflect for the most part but that it, indeed, reflects everything you said.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The interpreter said "zapitnik," and I don't understand that. What was meant by that, "zapisnik"? I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: What I wanted to ask, and I'll rephrase, did the testimony from the Milutinovic case reflect precisely and accurately what you have testified to in 2007 about the incidents in April 1999?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: With this explanation given -- I see my learned colleague on his feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do apologise. Perhaps the time is not right, but I believe it is. There is a problem in relation to 92 ter statements that are being admitted. What we get from the OTP is a list of exhibits that will be used, or, rather, exhibits that they will introduce through the witness, but they don't provide us with the 92 ter statement. So now we are admitting the Milutinovic transcript and the statement. The Defence does not prepare in the same way if only one statement is admitted or both. If the Trial Chamber believes that my proposal is appropriate, could the Prosecution please mark the statements that they are going to introduce as 92 ter statements. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm not sure that I fully understand the problem. Do you, Mr. Neuner? I gather that Mr. Djurdjic is saying he hasn't received a copy of the statements and of the transcript of evidence which you're now tendering.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise, Your Honour. You didn't quite understand me. What we get is a list of exhibits that the Prosecutor is going to use, but the Prosecutor does not mark the statement that will be tendered through Rule 92 ter. It's not marked. They give us four or five statements that will be used, but they don't say which one is going to be tendered as a 92 ter statement, whether it's going to be one, two, three, or four statements. For example, we had one statement of Witness Nike Peraj that was a 92 ter statement, but there were two or three others one there as well. Thank you. I think that you have understood what I'm saying right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And I think Mr. Neuner now does as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I wish to reply briefly. Because I'm aware about the time, and I'm almost afraid I can't make it within one hour now with all these objections. On the point, we have submitted a list and the 65 ter number, which I've also read out this morning, 2646, contained the following description: "Amended Rule 92 ter statement of K-6," it said in the description. We also provided the dates, including the date 31st of January, 2007, to this one. This is a Rule 92 ter witness, Your Honour. We have notified the Court in our filings about the fact that the status of this witness is a 92 ter witness, and we believe this, in itself, is self-explanatory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The important thing for the future, Mr. Neuner, and I'm sure that you and Mr. Stamp with Mr. Djurdjic and Mr. Djordjevic, can get a system that is clear and simple working, but the Defence seeks to be able to know which of the exhibit statements you provide is going to be the actual 92 ter statement. So if we can just leave it with you and Mr. Djurdjic to be sure that in future that is clear to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And now move on with speed, Mr. Neuner.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Have I asked that the testimony with the 65 ter number 5118 is being tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received, and that will need to be under seal?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Yes, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P00322, under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I will briefly read out the summary. "The witness, K90, is a VJ insider who was stationed in Djakovica in spring 1999. He was a military policeman in the 2nd Battalion of the 549th Motorised Brigade. His unit ordered Albanian villagers from villages around Djakovica to leave their homes based on his commander's order to relocate them. "The witness relates that in late April 1999 the VJ secured the area around the villages of Korenica and Meje. Around 400 additional PJP policemen arrived. The witness also saw some Frenki soldiers. The police entered the villages and fired randomly into houses. The witness saw burnt homes. As a result, large columns of refugees formed along the roads to Djakovica. "The witness observed that policemen separated Albanian men from women and led the men to a nearby yard. He saw several groups led to his house and heard shots -- led to this house and heard shots. Once he approached this yard where he was told by policemen that they were slaughtering Siptars. In a small house on the yard, he saw bodies covering the ground. Before leaving the police set fire to houses within the yard where Albanians had been killed. "The witness also accompanied some wounded VJ soldiers and a column of Albanian civilians towards Djakovica." If we could briefly move to private session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Among the command line, to whom did Mr. Nenad Nesovic report to?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the battalion, Major Vukovic. As for the security line, someone in Prizren. I don't know who.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And Mr. Vukovic, what was his exact position?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander of the 2nd Battalion of the 549th Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And Mr. Vukovic reported to whom?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: To then Colonel Delic, Bozidar Delic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And he was holding which position?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Commander of the 549th Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And to whom did Mr. Delic report to in 1999?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The corps commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Of which corps and what is it --

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Pristina Corps. The Pristina Corps, the commander was General Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I want to now have a map, 615.04 being displayed, please. And while this is being done, could we move to private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: You mention in your statement that the police arrived. When roughly, that day when you were at the command post, did the police arrive?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some police were already there, but others arrived around 7.00. I don't know exactly what time it was, but thereabouts, 7.00, 7.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: In the morning or in the evening?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And how did these additional policemen arrive?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: They arrived on buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: How many buses?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: About ten, plus or minus. Around ten, as far as I could see.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And how many persons were in each of these ten buses?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot really claim with any certainty, but about 40 of them. If they also had weapons and equipment with them, it would have been around 40 -- 35 to 40 men.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Thirty-five to 40 men per bus? Could you clarify, please.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And where did you see these buses going to? Could you mark that on the map.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. From Djakovica, headed towards Korenica, that was one group; whereas the other one was somewhere from this area, but I couldn't go any further up because I'm not sure. But it's approximately how far the buses could actually reach. Further on they couldn't go anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Could you mark on both arrows which you have just drawn a 2.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: In paragraph 48, the second sentence of your statement, you talk about the police, and you say, I quote, "They entered into villages and randomly fired into homes." Which villages are you referring to here?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm referring to Korenica primarily because that's what I did see. But it's possible that the other villages were also involved, but I was speaking of Korenica specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And you're stating "they randomly fired." What do you mean by "randomly"?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they stopped the vehicle, and then they would fire at the house which was there. They would fire with a machine-gun. This was not a classic combat vehicle, military vehicle, but it was like a jeep, an all-terrain vehicle, and they had a machine-gun mounted on it at that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Could you describe the colour of the vehicle?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the green military drab, camouflage. I can't describe it precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And who was operating the machine-gun?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The policeman who was on the vehicle, so the policeman fired from the vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: At that moment was there any outgoing fire from Korenica village proper?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: The whole morning, did you see any outgoing fire coming from Korenica, being directed outside, outwards?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: In paragraph 53 of your statement, you state, "Houses were burning all around." Could you describe where you saw burning houses that morning?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was on the approaches to Korenica village, the first part, the area that you can see here. All the houses were burning, including the one that was right here, the first house, up to this line here, which is as far as I went.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: You have marked now at the eastern border of Korenica some bold stricken line. Could you mark below that bold line a number 3, please.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: How far away from the burning houses was the command post where you were?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say with certainty, but about 120, 130 metres, maybe less. If we look at the first house that was here toward the command post, that house would have been around 100 metres from the command post, and the other houses were about 120 to 150 metres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: After the houses burned that day, did you ever at a later point in time return to Korenica?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a few days later, five, six, maybe ten days later, I did return. I don't know exactly what the date was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And how did the houses you saw in the village of Korenica, how did the houses look like there?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they were totally charred. There were no roofs anymore. They weren't really livable anymore, the houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: What do you mean by "livable"?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that means that they were with no roof; there were no windows or doors. Everything that could be consumed in a fire was consumed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: In paragraph 63, the second sentence of your statement, you're mentioning "I travelled with an ambulance," and you say, and I quote, "On the way I recall seeing some bodies on the side of the road near the entrance of Korenica." Could you mark for us the location where you saw these bodies by drawing a circle.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not on the side of the road. They were in the first house that I mentioned earlier, next to this fence here, in this part, at the very -- by the very entrance or approach to the village, maybe some 50 metres from the village itself. So the bodies were next to a fence there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Could you -- I know it's already relatively populated, the map, but could you try to mark it with a circle next to which you please add the number 4.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there's a blot here, but let me try and draw it. It's right here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And could you roughly mark a circle. Because you haven't marked a circle yet.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I did mark a circle. You can see it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Okay. What type of clothes wore the dead persons, the four dead persons, that day?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall the colour or what clothes they had on, but they were civilians, that's for sure. They didn't have uniforms on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Did you see any weapons lying next to the dead persons or in the hands of the dead persons?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: You also talk in your statement about two soldiers which were wounded and which you had to retrieve that day. Could you mark with a circle, adding the letter Q to it, where these two wounded soldiers were.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as there's a big blot here, I'll try to draw it. It should be on this thick line here, but I will mark it here, and it's approximately right there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Just for the explanation, because it's getting fuller and fuller, the witness has, below the road leading from Djakovica to Korenica, below the arrow which he has indicated with number 2, marked another circle and added below that circle the letter Q.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: With regard to paragraph 52 of your statement, you state that 500 displaced Albanian people from Korenica were proceeding in a column. Could you indicate by drawing an arrow in which direction the column of people from Korenica was moving.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that there were 500 people in one column. I said they were in several groups of 10, 20, or 30 people, and this was on several occasions. So they weren't all coming at once, together. And here, where I drew this house, well, let me draw this line here, so it was there. And also from this other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Can you -- can you, taking the arrow coming from Korenica, can you, at the beginning of the line leading to the arrow, mark the letter B, please, because there is some space left. The map is getting fuller.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Thank you. And this second arrow, I will just describe for the record. You have marked a line coming from Orize, hitting the main road from Korenica towards Djakovica. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Could you, maybe in the vicinity of the word "Orize" mark a C next to that line, if it's possible.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Orize.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Actually, maybe could I impose the goodwill of the usher, I wanted to make it 1:1, as the witness had marked it in his statement, but the letter C is so far away now. The map is too full. Could I ask the usher to remove the C, because it's too far away. It's not possible?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Okay, If it's not possible, could you from the letter C draw an arrow towards the direction in which the column was moving.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I did not want to intervene earlier, regardless of what these markings looked like. The witness wrote and marked what he said, and he marked it, and I think that there is no reason to delete it, although the Prosecutor considers it necessary. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The C is remaining and something further is being marked, as I understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: If it is possible, could you -- could you just explain what you mean by C. What -- you were talking about two columns. The column of Korenica we had. What did you want to indicate what you meant by the letter C? Could you just explain for the record.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: C is the Orize village. That's where the column was moving from the crossing in Orize towards the main road that was leading to Korenice and Junik.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Okay. Then in paragraph 54 and 55 of your statement, you mentioned that there were 30 policemen at the crossroad A who separated men from women and took them to the yard. Could you, first of all, indicate where you believe the crossroad A was?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Neuner, we have now got a map marked with so many things that it's going to be extremely difficult to make sense of it. If you want other positions marked, I think you need to start afresh on a new map.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I would ask that the map is then being tendered right now, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P00323, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I just want to make sure we don't get into a problem. My colleague Neuner began describing some letters referring to a map that is not this map but the map attached to the statement, and we had no opportunity to see that exhibit. And also the witness did not reply to that question because of Your Honour's intervention, and I just wanted to point out that if he were to answer the question relating to paragraphs 54 and 55, then we should see the map where those letters are marked, and I think this is in statement 4626 that was adopted or, rather, tendered as a 65 ter document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Mr. Djurdjic, but what I believe Mr. Neuner is about to do is to start with a clean map and have the position of those policemen at crossroad A marked on the new map, so I think that that should make it clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Could I just ask that after -- this map is obviously being tendered now, that we have the same map and the same enlargement again, please. It could even be a much broader enlargement. Just -- we don't need Djakovica, no. I think that's perfectly suitable.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Could you mark again with a circle the location of the VJ command post and add a "VJ" to the circle.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you now mark the crossroad where you saw 30 policemen by drawing a circle around the crossroad and adding a letter A south of it.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Could you mark a letter A below the circle.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Thank you. And could you now mark with the letter E, for Emil, where you believe the yard was to which the policemen took the separated men.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: The witness, for the record, has marked east of the crossroad a circle with a letter E on top of it. The letter E is not very legible.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: How many groups did you see being taken there at the end of April that day, 1999?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: And it wasn't that far.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Okay. But could you answer my question: How many groups did you see being led to this yard, which was not far away from the crossroad, at the end of April 1999?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we bear in mind that I was there three or four times, that means that this one group that came -- that arrived the latest, I can't tell you exactly how many men there were. But as they came, they would release some men, and some they would bring in. And what I could see was that they had brought at least three to four groups there. Well, some were going in one direction; others in another. In any case I wasn't really watching this because that wasn't my job. But there were certainly three to four groups, including the last group of which I'm certain that did go there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: So three to four groups at least. Could you say how many men, roughly, were in each of these groups?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's very difficult now to tell you, because it was a general commotion there at the crossroads, so I can't really tell you how many people were there, how many men. But I'm sure, and I'm certain for this last group, because I ran across -- I came across them as I was returning, there were about eight to ten men in the group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the witness said "three to four groups," that's what I saw, and then my learned colleague Neuner says, "So you saw at least three to four groups." I think that's inappropriate. If we heard the witness's answer, we should just move on, and I don't think anything can be accomplished by this kind of wording.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think it was an attempt by Mr. Neuner to reflect language which had been used earlier, which was "certainly three to four groups," and earlier than that it had been "at least three to four groups." They were the words of the witness, and that appears at line 2 of page 22, so I don't think we can be at all critical of that, Mr. Djurdjic. Yes, Mr. Neuner.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: But I will just clarify the point raised by my learned colleague.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Witness, how many groups do you, today, remember having seen being led to that house?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: At least four. So if I went there on three occasions and one group that I met on the way, so that's four groups, so at least four.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: You say you went there on three occasions. What do you mean? Where did you go on three occasions?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The crossroads. I meant being at the crossroads, going from the command post to the crossroads that was marked with the letter A.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And whom did you see at the crossroads from the Serbian side? What persons from the Serbian side did you see at this crossroad?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not understand your questions, but if you mean policemen, yes, I did see policemen at the crossroads. I don't know what you mean by "the Serbian side."

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I meant policemen, but I didn't want to lead you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I want to now move into private session for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P00324, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Could we now have Exhibit -- 65 ter number 1326 on our screens, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I want you now to give us some description about the policemen which you saw in and around Korenica and at the yard. We have here a photo-board containing several uniforms for you. Could you please by looking at this, and you see the numbers here, tell the Court which type of uniform wore the policemen that arrived in the ten buses that morning?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There's a first question before that one, Mr. Neuner, whether the policemen who arrived that morning in the buses were wearing any of the types of uniforms shown on this photo-board.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Okay, yeah. I will proceed as suggested.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Could you, first of all, tell me whether the policemen were wearing any type of uniform, who arrived -- the policemen who arrived this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that it would be proper for the witness to first describe the uniforms and then to have the uniforms displayed so that he could then indicate which ones he recognises. That would be the right procedure to follow, if something is to be recognised. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That would be a correct procedure, Mr. Djurdjic, but the one I've suggested, I think, will suffice in the circumstances. The question, though, to be asked is whether the uniforms depicted on this board, whether any one of those was the type being worn that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Could I go now step by step? Did you see any of the policemen wearing uniforms that morning? And I'm talking to the policemen in the bus?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Could you describe what you saw, what colour of the uniform they had.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, classical blue uniform with vests, combat vests, on which it said "PJP," special police unit. That was on the back. Well, you can't really see it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I would now, just for -- to get the first questions in, move on to the policemen which you saw three or four times at the crossroads. You marked the crossroad as A on the map. Did you see these policemen wearing any uniform, and how would you describe it?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, just like a minute ago, but it is these under number 6 that are the closest to the type of uniform that those people wore.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I don't want you to touch for the time being the photo-board. I want to now move on to the main policemen to whom you spoke in the yard of the house you marked as E, for Emil. Did this man wear a uniform, or didn't he? And how would you describe it?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, like the previous ones. Classical police uniform with a combat vest.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Okay. Could you now look at the photo-board in front of you, and, as far as I understood you, you had summarised that they all looked similar, meaning the policemen in the bus, at the crossroad, A, and in the yard, E --

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I can withdraw that if my learned colleague has ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If my colleague is withdrawing his question, then there's no reason for me to object.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I withdraw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Witness, I start afresh. Could you, looking at this photo-board, please tell us which of the uniform types, if any, resemble the closest the policemen who arrived in the buses that morning?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, perhaps I'm a bit of a bore, but now my learned friend, the Prosecutor, is trying to gear the witness's clear answers in the direction that he wants them to be geared towards. The witness said three times what kind of uniforms the policemen wore, and now my colleague is trying to deal with the policemen one by one, yet again, to ask what kind of uniforms they wore. I don't think that's right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Neuner.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I have now followed, I believe, a proper procedure, as suggested, and I have asked some founding questions relating to this photo-board, and I'm now trying to finally move towards the photo-board itself. On this photo-board there are ten different uniforms depicted. I believe I'm now authorised to ask the witness to pick, if he can, one or several of the pictures which resemble the persons I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Continue, please, Mr. Neuner.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Now, my question was: The policemen who arrived that morning in buses, if you look at the photo-board in front of you, which one of the pictures, if any, resembles the closest the uniforms worn by the policemen in the bus?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The one on the photograph that is marked number 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: If I now move on to the about 30 policemen who were stationed that day at the crossroad you marked as letter A on the map a minute ago, which one of the ten pictures, if any, resembled the closest the uniform worn by these 30 policemen?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Photograph number 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: If I then move on to the policemen you spoke to in the yard of the house you marked as letter E on the previous map, which one of the ten uniforms, if any, resembled the closest the uniforms worn by these policemen?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Photograph number 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And the other nine policemen you also saw in the yard of the house marked as E, how would you describe this uniform, if you look at the pictures here in front of you.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, photograph number 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I would ask that the picture is being tendered, Your Honour, the photo-board.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The photo-board will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P00325, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And could I ask you what weapons the 30 policemen wore at the crossroad A, when you passed by that day?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Automatic rifles that regular police officers have.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And the weapons worn by the policemen in the yard you described with the letter E on your map.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Would you be in a position to pick the type of weapon out of a photo-board, if I show you one, a photo-board of weapons?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: If I could ask that the 65 ter number 1323 is being shown to this witness. It has two pages. We would go for the first page, and after a few seconds I would ask that it be -- the page is being flipped. I'm sorry, it was 1324. If we could, now that we have had a few seconds, move to the second page. Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Photograph number 1. I beg your pardon, weapon number 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: So we are now on the second page with the ERN number K0218271, and you believe that the policemen at the crossroad and in the yard wore weapon number 1, is it?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.
