utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: What type of weapon, if you can recall, is this?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Automatic rifle. M-84 -- no, no, wait a minute. I can't remember now. I've forgotten. I know, but at this moment I've forgotten totally, because I had one just like it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: So you, being a member of the VJ, you also had a similar weapon; yeah?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm saying the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Could I ask that this exhibit is being tendered, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P00326, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Did you observe any insignia worn by the policemen at the crossroads or at -- in the yard?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's just what they have on their sleeves and what it says on the combat vests, if that's what you meant. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Could you describe what was on this insignia depicted?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, "Police" on the sleeve and then on the combat vest where the ammunition clips in the back, where that little bag is, up there it says "Posebne jedinice," or something like that. At any rate, there is big white letters, Cyrillic letters.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And what colour?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Green. Green. The vests are green, and the uniforms are blue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And the insignia, what colour?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The insignia are white on the sleeve and on the back of the vest.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Could we have a look at Exhibit 1323, please, 65 ter number 1323.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do beg your pardon, Your Honour, but again we have a problem. What is being displayed is something that is supposed to be recognised, and beforehand it has not been described, especially when we have this kind of exhibit in front of us where it is actually written what is what. I mean, if something is being described, then it should be described first and only then the witness can recognise what it is that he is supposed to recognise. I believe that that would be the only right course to take.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: As I have understood it, there has been a description. Whether that description is reflected in any of these pictures is another question. Carry on, please, Mr. Neuner.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Could you indicate, among the 13 insignia here in front of you, which one of these 13 closely resembles, if any, closely resembles the insignia you saw that day at the policemen at the crossroad A?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Seven. Seven. The rest is mostly military, as far as I could see.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Could I also ask you, within the yard, which of the insignia worn most closely resembled --

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: We need to have the insignia back, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: -- the insignia worn by the policemen in the yard?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, number 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Thank you. You are familiar with the other insignia. Could you explain for us if you know any other insignia here?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: We need, please, both.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the most part, those that are for the army. As for the others, well, I don't know. The military ones, for the most part.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Which one do you recognise?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Photograph number 3, photograph number 1, photograph number 4, the one that I had, too. I don't know about the others. Well, number 7, as I've already said. As for the others, well, these are some --

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Can we have the first --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Can you explain to us which unit wore insignia number 1, please?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, sorry. Of course you can see it written here, the 63rd Airborne. You can see it written there. The question is from what time this is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Do you know from which time it is?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. Well, maybe I could remember, but it's still a question -- well, all of it is -- I don't know, I don't know. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Could you explain to us what number 4, insignia number 4, is?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Military police insignia. I don't know if it's still the same. It was changed before that and after that every year, so now I really don't know which ones -- well, I mean at that moment it was this one, but now I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: "At that moment," which year are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The war years. Well, that would be around, say, from the 1990s up to 1999, 2000. It changed a lot. While I worked for the military, at least two or three insignia were changed. I can't even remember now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: But in 1999, you, yourself, had insignia number 4?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Number 4, that's right. Yes, it's on the photograph there, the one that I gave you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I would seek this exhibit to be tendered, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P00326, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: You mention in paragraph 66 of your statement that the policemen withdrew an hour before the VJ troops. Could you explain how the police withdrew that day?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Got onto the buses and left.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: So how many buses did you see? Where did the buses pick them up, and where did they -- in which direction did the buses go?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the same place that they had come from but in the opposite direction; the same number of buses, what I said, around ten, well, give or take one or two.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And in which direction did the buses leave?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some were going from Korenica towards Djakovica. Others passed by that crossroad where they collected those 30 or so. They also took the road towards Djakovica. I don't know about after that, but they took the road leading to Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And what -- in what condition was the compound, you marked as E for Emil a moment ago, when the police left?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they burnt the house, the little house there. The main house in the yard was not set on fire. Only the little one that was in the yard. Actually, there was yet another one there, but it wasn't really a little house. It was something like made of wood, but that was not torched.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Did you at any point in time return towards the house -- I'll stop. I withdraw that. When did you, yourself, leave?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Around 4.00 in the afternoon. Between 3.30 and 4.00, 4.30, it would be that period of time, sort of.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And did somebody leave with you, or you left everybody behind at the command post?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We all withdrew, at that point in time, that is, all of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And the house was still burning at this point in time?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Did you at any point in time return to that house?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the following day.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And what did you observe?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just the foundations, the other layer there, and nothing else. Nothing else was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Did you see any traces of bodies which you had seen lying in the small house?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nothing, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Did you see any ashes or any burned traces?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing, absolutely nothing. Absolutely nothing, that is to say, absolutely nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Were there any troops in the area when you returned?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I note the time. I would just have one more map which I hope to squeeze in. If we could have Exhibit 615.4, that's the map, being displayed again.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And I just want you to mark one area. You mentioned in your statement, in paragraph 44, that your unit was involved in the relocation of nine to ten villages and hamlets. Could you explain to us - we don't need to have it enlarged - could you explain to us, where were these nine to ten hamlets and villages located?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said nine to ten hamlets, not villages. One of the villages is Zub; here it is. The other village is Brekovac, part of Brekovac, rather, and the hamlets around there. Not villages, not nine or ten villages, no. Do we understand each other now?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: We perfectly do. Could you roughly mark by drawing a broader arrow the area where these hamlets were located, nine to ten hamlets?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, everywhere around here, sort of here, and then this part, and then here by the cemetery here, and here by the river.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: So the witness has marked some six, seven, circles where he believed that the villages -- or hamlets were.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Three, four, five, six, seven, eight.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Yes, which were relocated.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Could you tell me which time period the relocation was taking place?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. From the beginning of April onwards. I can't remember exactly what the time was because, well -- in that period, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: In which year?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I would seek this -- to tender this map, Your Honours, and at this point in time the Prosecution has no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: This will be received, and it should be 328.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could we mention that at page 34, line 19, the previous exhibit, I think, is incorrectly noted as P326. It should be P327. Mr. Neuner, that was an improvement over previous performances, but still not within time, so there is room for continued improvement.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I got a couple of objections, Your Honour, which needed time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We are aware of that so we let you run on a little, yes. We now need to take the second break, and we'll resume at 12.30.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Djurdjic, you have some cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Witness, my name is Veljko Djurdjic, and I'm a member of the Defence team of the accused Vlastimir Djordjevic, and Jelena Dzambazovic a member if the team is also with me, whereas Mr. Djordjevic Dragoljub is absent, and his absence is excused. Before we begin, since we are speaking the same language, in order to be efficient, I would urge you to pay attention to the questions that I put to you, wait for me to finish, and then provide an answer so that the interpreters have an opportunity to interpret it in due time. Mr. Witness, may I address you in this fashion? I would like to start by asking you about your evidence today. You have made many statements, and there were many problems with all those statements, but right now at the outset I would like to put a few questions to you, and please tell me why this is so: First of all, can you -- do you have a recollection of the events that you are testifying about? Is your recollection better now or at the time when you made your statements in December 2002?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the changes to my statements had to do with the wording, mainly. Generally speaking, the events that I testified about --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Please, listen to my question. I'm just asking you, is your memory better today, as you are testifying, or in 2002 when you made the statement?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: My memory and my recollection of the events is the same, both now and then.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: All right. Now let me ask you something else. You mentioned several things today that you have not mentioned before, not in the statements that you made to the Prosecutor on the 8th and -- 7th and 8th of February, and I will point out those differences, and you tell me why these omissions. The first thing that you mentioned for the first time in your supplemental sheet of 19 February 2009, was this vehicle with a mounted machine-gun, a green-coloured vehicle, and you said that there was a policeman on that vehicle. That's the first thing. The second thing you mentioned for the first time is that you went back to Korenice five or six days later and then you saw what you saw in the village. And then toward the end of your evidence today, you said that you were also in Korenice the next day, the following day, and that's when you saw what you saw. So how do you explain this, the first mention of these things in -- on the 18th and 19th of February, 2009, and not having mentioned that before?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me begin with the first thing. The house we are talking about --

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, can I just interrupt before the witness is answering. I believe that this witness has not stated he went back to Korenica the next days. If I remember correctly, he stated in his evidence he went back a couple of days, about a week later, to Korenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That is not my recollection, Mr. Neuner. I think Mr. Djurdjic is quoting the evidence correctly. Thank you. Carry on, please, Mr. Djurdjic. The witness was in the process of answering.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I'll start with the last question. The house that I mentioned -- that I marked on the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, please just answer my questions. There is no need for you to repeat your evidence. I quoted your words. You said for the first time the things that you mentioned in the -- to the Prosecutor on the 18th and 19th, 2009. How come you said these things for the first time now, without -- failing to mention them in 2002?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably no one asked me about these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I take notes during the evidence in chief, and I put questions based on those notes, and I can only make an error by omission. I'm just saying this for the benefit of my learned colleague Neuner.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mentioned my name.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Carry on, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, speaking of the supplemental information sheet of 18th or 19th February, 2009, tell me, please, have you read in the Serbian language the statement that was compiled and that is part of the evidence that was entered into evidence?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: When do you mean have I read it?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Well, on the 18th and 19th of February.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's move on. You state that you were born on the date as stated. Just tell me, please, your mother and father, did you live in the same household?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As of 1983 -- as of 1983, no, but we still have a joint household. I still have a joint household with my brothers, but we all live in different areas. My brother lives in one town, my other brother in another, and I live in a third place, so that's about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me what schools you completed?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: High school.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Where and when?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1978, 1979, in Lebane.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me, did you serve in the army immediately after your high school, or did you get a job?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first I went to do my compulsory military service. Yes, that was first.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me, sir, when and where did you complete your military service, and what is your military specialty?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in Lebane. In 1981, I finished, I completed my military service. I was serving on the border at the time. My military specialty at the time was 11-107. And when I was employed in the army, I was in the military police, and my military specialty was VES-101, or 11-101, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic, we are getting a lot of potentially identifiable material. If you're pursuing this line, we should move into private session. The witness is protected and no identifying material should be in the public record.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I understood, but I thought that these were general questions that cannot identify the witness because every man who -- every healthy man of military age serves in the army. But I will be careful, and I will address Your Honours with a special request for a closed session if there are some details that are going to be revealed by the witness that could identify him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Now, Witness, please, you answered my question, but just tell me this: When you returned from the army, where were you -- where were your military records?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Lebane.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: My military records are still in Lebane.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In order to avoid mentioning details, I would like to ask you this --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, could we please move into closed session, just for this basic general information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Witness, do you know that NATO aircraft were guided in the following way: On the Albania side of the border, there would be fires; and on our side of the border, light signals were emitted.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is possible, but I did not see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Am I right if I say that NATO bombed every day?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. Several times, as a matter of fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Am I right that you stated here that it happened at least twice a day and sometimes even more, even 10 to 12 times a day?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Twice" would be too mild.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Tell me, from the time when you came to the area, did you have any conflicts with the KLA, and where was the KLA then?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was at Pastrik that we had our most conflict, when they took this big rock out there, and then a guide from Leskovac got killed then. At any rate, they'd start shooting, and then they'd run away, and then they would start shooting, and then they'd run away. So that would be about it. There wasn't any direct combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember that there were incursions from the territory of the Republic of Albania into our territory and that there was fighting there and -- please answer.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if we exclude the situation, I mean what happened at Pastrik and Kosur, in other places there were only minor incidents. Kosur and -- what was the name? Oh, the place next to Prizren, I can't remember now. Was it Planeja? I think that that would be right. I don't think that I've made a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, did you have occasion to see tanks of the Republic of Albania and their participation in these incidents?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, I saw them several times. I don't know whose tanks they were. I don't know whose tanks they were, but I did see tanks several times. And they consciously came to the border in order to provoke a possible answer on the part of our army. I saw them personally. At that time I was escorting Major Vukovic. I went to the border very often and practically on a regular basis I saw them there, moving in the territory of Albania, I mean towards the border, towards the border with us, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Am I right if I say that you believed, or, rather, you said that in your statements, that our troops were present at the border in very small numbers? And in view of this opinion of yours, why do you actually think so?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, we weren't afraid of the Albanians that were on the other side there at all. There could be strikes that would come from NATO. There might be a ground invasion. I mean, if there were to be initial combat, well, I don't think that with that many people you could stop a land force that would be on the move with lots of equipment. But perhaps in terms of initial fighting, well, yes. I mean, have I clarified this now?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Now that you've mentioned Pastrik, I would like to ask you whether perhaps you were in Kosur?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was, one day and one night.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: May I conclude that that was also with the 2nd Motorised --

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, am I right, and do you remember, that at the Cafa Pruse boarder crossing, sometime towards the end of March, there were quite a few civilians of Albanian ethnicity? And do you remember that your commander went there, that part of the territory was de-mined so that they could pass through that area? They insisted that they should cross over, and you helped them cross safely?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you give me a minute so I can explain how this went. A group of Albanians that was coming from the direction of Suva Reka and from areas around Djakovica, I simply don't know on whose orders, but I claim that none of us said that to them, they set out for Albania. And then there was this very unpleasant situation. There's aircraft that keep bombing all the time. On the other side there are minefields, and they had almost entered the minefields. The commander asked these people, I was there, to stay on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Please slow down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, I really am sorry. I do really do apologise. The commander asked these people to stay there. We gave them food and water until these minefields were removed. All these people who came from the interior of Kosovo, from any side, and who had passed part of the territory that was under the control of the 2nd Battalion of our unit, had water, food. We gave them everything that we could at that moment. Now, whether they asked for that or not, I mean, that didn't really matter. There were always people who gave them food and water. I want to say that in Djakovica there was this kiosk where there were --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. You have answered my question. Thank you. Witness, am I right that if I say that at the time when you came to Djakovica and to the border area, that due to NATO bombing the locals from Deva, Guska, Babaj Boks, Lepovac, Grcin, Rogovo, Kusnin, and Damjanin, left their villages and went to Djakovica and Prizren?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, when I arrived there and when I first went to that side, I mean facing the Deva border post, these people had already left. I did not see them. They had probably left while I was still in Zub, while our command most was still in Zub. They had probably left earlier on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Am I correct in saying that the reasons why these Albanian civilians left their villages in the border areas were the fear of bombing, the fear of expected fighting between the KLA and the Yugoslav Army, and fear of the KLA itself?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is quite possible that you are right. For those people that we helped -- that I know of who were transferred, as a soldier, as a regular soldier --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Please just answer whether I'm right or not. Just say yes or no so that we can move on, because, you know, our time here is limited. We cannot just chat here.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is very difficult to answer with a yes or no. If I say yes, then my answer is incomplete, and if I say no, my answer is again incomplete.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Well, if you can answer with yes, then others will continue on with questions and ask you about it.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, but that's not the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there is that possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, do you know that NATO aircraft fired on civilians in Gato [phoen], Meja, and the refugee centre on the Meje-Djakovica-Junik road.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in Meje, I'm sure of that. As for the other places, I don't know. In Bistrazin, yes. In Meje, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you aware that villagers from the bordering villages, on the borders with the Republic of Albania, in the villages of Vlahan, Dogra, and Zogaj, also withdrew from this territory so they wouldn't be near the border with Serbia?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, from what we could observe from our border post, there were no Albanians on the Albanian side, so I don't know -- but I don't know what happened there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now I would just have something to ask you about. Do you know that at your command post in Prekovo --

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Prekovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Prekovac, I apologise. All this time there was a group of Albanian civilians, and they stayed there until the end of the war together with you.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, we were in a village. If you mean policemen, Albanian policemen, General Djordjevic will be better placed to explain what men these were. Now do you remember when there was -- for a time there was unit of police that was formed, their unit of police. But I don't know exactly how it went, but they had weapons, and they took care of the civilians. But to make a long story short, they were there together with the civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Did you understand my question? I was asking you: Did Albanian civilians remain in -- at your command post throughout the war, there together with you?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but not only Albanian civilians, sir. There were also Serbs from Prekovac and other villages who also withdrew to this area. Not only Serbs but also Roma people, they all came there to be with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know whether your commander established a platoon for the protection of civilians? Please, if you do know, just don't mention any names.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: If what you mean by that is a description of the houses where people stayed and lived, maybe that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: No. Listen to my question. Do you know whether your commander had established a platoon for civilian protection?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know. Maybe.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that in early April, during the transfer of the command post to the Prekovac village, you found an old man who was bed-ridden of Albanian ethnicity and that you called an ambulance to transfer him to a hospital?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I participated in this -- in this operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would have a new set of questions, and they have to do with your statements to the Prosecutor. Tell me, please, how did you get in touch with the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was very difficult. I actually reported to them. I was really sorry that we withdrew from Kosovo, and then I contacted the Prosecution because I wanted the whole thing to be clarified with the late President Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now let's just clarify one thing. While you were being proofed for today's evidence, were you shown any documents?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only my statement, if you mean that by "documents."

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Other than that, any other documents, any maps or sketches?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. Maybe the sketch that I made, that I drew when I was here last, 1997, maybe. I don't know, maybe there was an error in that sketch but --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. That's enough. Let's move on. According to our information, you gave your first statement on the 7th and 8th of December, in 2002.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's possible. I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, when you gave that statement, who was present during your giving of the statement?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know who the Prosecutor and the investigator was, but I don't know who the interpreter was. I know there was this investigator John Zdrilic, but I don't recall the name of the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: How many days did this take, your witness interview?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Was the same interpreter present throughout the interview?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you're asking now that I remember something that happened ten years ago. I really would love to help, but I can't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm asking you whether you can remember now because I'd like to remind you of what you said while you were testifying in the Milutinovic case.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Well, please do repeat what you can remember.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think it was not the same interpreter throughout who was present during this interview, but it does mean that it was not the same person. I think it wasn't the same woman, but I'm not absolutely certain. I can only say yes or no, but I have no proof. I can't remember the name of the interpreter, and that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, do you remember anything else that you said during the proofing in the Milutinovic case, or would you like me to refresh your memory by reading it to you?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, could we please see on the screens Exhibit -- a Prosecution Exhibit number 5118 on the 65 ter list, and if it's easier, I can also quote the D number. I don't know what is easier. Mr. Registrar, what is the faster way?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: This is a transcript from a previous trial. You'll have to be careful in what questions you ask from that because of the content of some of it. It will not appear on the screens outside of this courtroom, but your questions could be disclosing some material in it that's important.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I took a look at my notes, and I think there are -- I think I have only two names, two investigators, and the name of an interpreter. There are no other names, but I will be careful.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Witness, please be careful. Do not mention any name. So this was the 30th of January, 2007, page 9367, lines 13 through 25.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Your Honour, when I made my statement to the investigator, there was only one investigator and this woman. Not the woman who signed the woman but another woman. And from time to time a man would come in. He said what his name was, but I can't remember it. He was only there occasionally, not throughout the interview." In response to the Judge's question, whether it was true that the witness had been read back to you in your language, you said: "I don't recall that it had been read back to me on that day, but when I signed it, it may have or may not have. But if that was the case, I'd like to correct it. And had been read back to me, I would have corrected it. I'm certain of that. So I don't recall the statement being read to me." And then on page 9368, lines 14 through 23, in response to the Judge's question: "Is it possible that the statement was made on one day. On the following day it was read over to you, and you signed it." So this is on page 9368, lines 13 to 14: "No, no, no. Not the next day, I'm sure, because the gentleman who took the statement went back to his country, and then they came back again. It was the new year, and then we saw each other in January or February, I don't know exactly when, in front of Hotel M or in a park; if it was the same day, in one of the parks in Belgrade, but certainly not in the Tribunal office in Belgrade. I was there only once, and it was then that the young lady who signed the statement was there. The first time it was another lady from Belgrade. I am certain about that." And then on page 9473, this is 65 ter 5118, 31st of January, 2007: "I signed a statement. I don't recall. It was either in Hotel M or in the park between Slavija and the government building of the Republic of Serbia, somewhere in that area, if this was on the same day. I don't know if it was on the same day. I'm not sure. I had not finished giving my statement at this time, and the woman from Belgrade was there who translated this statement. And then when I signed the statement, when I brought the photographs, there was a totally different interpreter and a completely different man, not the man who interviewed me in the beginning. This man could speak a little Serbian, too, not only English, because he was born -- I think he's a Croat, but he lives in Australia. I think that his name," and I'm not going to read the name, "I don't know. I'm not sure. I think that's the name." Now I've read all the answers that you gave in the Milutinovic trial. Have I jogged your memory?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And let me put another thing to you. When, toward the end of the trial, Mr. Hannis told you the name of the first investigator and the second investigator - and again I'm not going to mention their names because they might identify you - could you tell me now in relation to this, since I jogged your memory, could you explain how everything happened and where you actually signed the statement.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The gentleman I'm referring to, and from you read, the man that you said could speak Serbian, that's the man I gave the statement to. But as far as I can remember, I signed that statement where you said, where you read that I had signed it. But now this was about seven years ago, so it's hard to remember. But I am sure that I signed the statement where you said, in the park.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Witness, please, let's clarify this. Based on what I read to you, on the first day when you made your statement, you didn't sign anything. Not only that you didn't sign anything, we also know the date on the statement. There were two dates, 7th and 8th of December, and you said that you only -- that this interview was only on one day, but that's irrelevant. But then you said that in January, February, some other men came and "then I signed the statement."

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't remember signing the statement on the first occasion; I still think I didn't. But as for the second occasion, that's correct, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: But, Witness, you also said that you will speak the truth in the Milutinovic case, and I was just quoting what you said there. So you said that at least two days later you signed the statement, but then I will remind you of other words that you said. But is this correct? First let me ask you this: Is what I read to you from the Milutinovic trial correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't remember what it was that I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Well, it was on the screen right now, and I also read it out to you.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's possible that you read it to me, but I don't remember. I know that I did sign one statement, and it's possible that it was a month or a month and a half later, that's what I said then. It's possible that I signed the statement then.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Is the -- is your evidence in the Milutinovic trial true and accurate?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I move to enter this -- well, actually, the entire transcript has already been tendered into evidence, so there is no need to propose its admission into evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, could we just take a short five-minute break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. We will need to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Witness, please do not mention any names. Tell me, tell me your opinion about your commander, your war-time commander, as a commander and as a human being.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what can I say? I can only say all the best. He's an excellent man, an excellent superior. All the best. I can only use superlatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, is it true, is it correct, that when you came to the town where you spent your war time, that the commander told you when you arrived that orders had to be complied with, that discipline has to be respected, and that everyone who engages in illegal actions will be taken to disciplinary -- will be disciplined and that measures will be taken against them?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: While we were still on the buses we were told that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We will do this later because I have to mention a name, and I don't want to go into closed session now. I'll skip this part. Let's take a look at paragraph 35 of your statement. Let me just remind you, it's about the cafe in Brekovac where you were --

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not sitting there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm sorry, then, you'll have to correct me. But one of your superiors was there and two inspectors?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and two other soldiers, but I wasn't there at the time. I was nearby but not at the cafe itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: While reading your statement in paragraph 35, one could conclude - and I don't want to read it out because of the name mentioned there - but one can conclude that you were there, too, and the other three and perhaps two or three other men. You mention also some other names there. If you weren't there, would you tell us how all this transpired and how you learnt about it?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the cafe was here, and right next to it was another room where I was, not in the cafe itself, but it was on the same premises, in the same building. I was just a wall behind them. So I had some other business to take care of, so I didn't sit with them. And I'm also -- I don't drink, so that's why I wasn't with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't say you were drinking --

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm just saying I'm not a drinker, I don't drink alcohol, so I wasn't sitting with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that that man and the two inspectors were drunk on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would be interested in the following: Who gave this initiative to go and find the person who was being searched for?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Am I right when I say that when you went to the third house in Djakovica, that you were actually ambushed and that fire was opened at you, and on that occasion one of these persons was injured?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't an ambush. It was a man. Now, was it the man we were looking for or not, but anyway, it was someone who was shooting.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that I can mention the name of the witness -- or, rather, the name of the person, the person who is suspected of having opened fire on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Witness, will you agree with me that this person was a member of the KLA, Chopi Albin [phoen]?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't remember the name, but I don't rule that possibility out. We were looking for a particular man, 20-something, but I cannot remember his name now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I know the name of the inspector who was injured on that occasion. Would it mean anything to you if I were to give you his name and surname?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you know that the investigating judge of the municipal court in Djakovica went out there and that a record was made of the on-site investigation with regard to the wounding of the inspector?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: The following day.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure that nothing like that took place that night. I don't know about the next day.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Is it true that immediately after the wounding an air-strike started?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps a minute or two later, so it was precisely that part of Cabrat that was being bombed, and we barely made it to down there where the church is. We took these streets and bombs were falling all over the place. So I don't know how many minutes had actually elapsed, but it was a very, very short time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to go back to paragraph 35 again. I'm not going to mention the name and surname of that officer who proposed that you immediately go to that address of that man that was known until then and to arrest him. Do you agree that this is incorrect in your statement?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: What?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: The statement says the name and surname of that officer, suggested that we go to the address of that person that was known until then and to arrest him straight away. It wasn't his initiative, and the statement seems to suggest that it was his initiative.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot really find where that is written. Could you tell me what paragraph that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 35, and the sentence is --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please slow down for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: In the fourth sentence, but the second part of it. Don't mention the last name, though.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't really understand this at all. What it says here, the first three -- uh-huh, I'm sorry. It says here: "The first three were fairly drunk when the conversation turned to the police attempts to locate an Albania man from Cabrat."

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Please read on.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Very unprofessionally, and I think only because he was drunk --"

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Don't mention the last name.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: " [Previous translation continues] ... suggested that we immediately attend the known addresses for this man and arrest him ..." Uh-huh, now I understand your question. I think that that is a consequence of what he had agreed to, I mean the policemen who were sitting with him beforehand.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I'm putting the question to you: Did he suggest to you that you go there or somebody else?

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The policeman suggested that, and he accepted.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: So it's not true that he's the one who suggested it. That's what's written here.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, possibly, possibly it's incorrect. Well, if that's what's written there, yes, yes. Oh, yeah, here it says the name suggested -- oh, okay, so that's not correct. I mean, it should have said "agreed."

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: In relation to him that's quite a difference.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes, a very important difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Well, I think it's very important to be accurate.

utterances.speaker: NIKE PERAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Agreed." "Agreed" would be the right word. I mean the proposal, the suggestion, had come from the other side, so it would be right to say "agreed." See, I read this statement so many times, and I simply -- well, this never really crossed my mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Witness, there are going to be other occasions to correct your statement --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I'm afraid that our tapes will run out, Your Honours and ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Djurdjic. We now need to adjourn for the day. Our next sitting, I believe, is on Wednesday, in the afternoon, so that we must adjourn until then. I'm afraid we've got to adjourn now, and we continue on Wednesday. The Court Officers will assist you in the time in between.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 25th day of February, 2009, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.46 p.m.,
